definition: An operation treated as one indivisible transition at the relevant concurrency boundary. State which storage or synchronization mechanism supplies that boundary.
A mechanism that reduces upstream production or admission when downstream capacity is limited. The contract must say whether callers wait, slow down, retry later, or receive rejection.
The resource or coordination boundary currently limiting the measured workload. Adding capacity elsewhere does not necessarily improve throughput. The bottleneck can move after a change.
A queue with an explicit capacity or admission limit. It bounds memory and waiting exposure; it does not increase the service rate or eliminate overload.
Making a derived cached value unusable after a change. An invalidation can race with an older fill, so ordering and version checks matter.
Many callers simultaneously regenerate missing or expired cached data. Coalesced fills, bounded admission, and carefully permitted stale serving can protect the authority.
An application reads a cache, loads a miss from its authority, and may populate the cache. Concurrent fills and writes need a stated freshness and invalidation policy.
A request to stop work that is no longer needed. Each stage must cooperate and release resources; a committed external effect may still need reconciliation.
Checking the peer’s certificate and the expected service identity under a trust policy. Encryption without authenticating the intended endpoint does not establish who receives the plaintext.
A load model in which each simulated user waits before issuing its next request. It can represent real interaction, but slower responses may reduce offered load.
The number of operations in progress at once. Operations can overlap while taking turns on one CPU; concurrency does not by itself imply simultaneous execution.
Stopping new work while allowing bounded in-flight work to finish before closing a process or connection. Long-lived clients need an explicit reconnect and recovery plan.
A bounded set of reusable connections. Waiting for the pool is queueing; multiplying per-instance limits during scale-out can overwhelm the dependency.
The dependent chain of work that determines completion time. Independent branches can overlap; sequential dependencies accumulate.
Pagination using a stable ordering position instead of only a numeric offset. Define tie-breakers, mutation behavior, expiry, and authorization of the cursor.
The time by which a caller no longer finds a result useful. Propagate a remaining budget to downstream work. Deadline expiry does not prove a previously sent mutation rolled back.
The naming system used to retrieve records such as addresses for a hostname. Resolution may involve cached answers and referrals; it is separate from an already-established application connection.
A mechanism that schedules asynchronous work and callbacks. Blocking CPU or synchronous I/O in the loop can delay unrelated requests; asynchronous syntax alone does not make the work nonblocking.
Feedback tied to actual submitted work, concrete excerpts, and an explicit rubric. A total score is derived from recorded dimensions and is not a hiring guarantee.
A set of components that may fail together because they share a dependency, location, power supply, runtime, or administrative action. Count independent domains rather than replica labels.
An intermediary acting on behalf of clients toward other services, such as an organization’s outbound proxy. The term describes its role.
An observable capability, such as creating a reservation or reading a message history. State who performs the action, its inputs, and its expected result.
Progress waits for earlier required work. TCP byte ordering can hold later bytes behind a gap; an HTTP/2 application stream and a transport byte stream have different ordering boundaries.
Adding instances or partitions. It helps only when work and state can be distributed and remaining shared resources have capacity.
A logical request/response channel multiplexed within an HTTP/2 connection. Independent streams still share transport behavior and resource limits.
A stable operation identity used to recognize retries and return or reconcile a durable result. Define its scope, retention, request-fingerprint checks, and transaction boundary.
An operation whose intended effect is the same when applied repeatedly with the same meaning. This does not promise identical responses or make all surrounding side effects safe.
A condition that must remain true across every allowed state transition. For a lending service: one physical copy has at most one active loan. Name the authority and atomic operation that protect it.
Assignment based on transport/network information, often at connection or flow granularity. Equal connection counts do not imply equal request cost.
Routing using application information such as an HTTP hostname or path. Access to encrypted application data generally requires an appropriate TLS termination boundary.
Elapsed time between a defined start and end of an operation. End-to-end latency includes relevant queueing, service, dependency, and network time. State the measurement boundary.

For a stable system with consistent boundaries, average work in progress equals average throughput times average time in the system: L = λW. Use matching units and do not treat an unstable, growing backlog as steady state.
A measurable quality or constraint: latency, availability, durability, privacy, cost, or an operational limit. “Fast” becomes useful only after defining a workload and threshold.
A load model that schedules arrivals independently of prior completions, within generator capacity. It can expose backlog growth that a waiting-client loop may suppress.
A stated multiplier from an average arrival rate to a modeled busy interval. It is an assumption to validate, not a universal constant for all products.

A boundary in an ordered sample distribution. A p95 below 200 ms describes approximately 95% of the measured population under the chosen convention; it does not bound every request. Do not average instance percentiles into a fleet percentile.
A client repeatedly asks for current state. Average request rate is approximately active clients divided by the polling interval, before retries and synchronization effects.
An operating-system execution context with its own resources and address-space boundary. Separate processes provide useful isolation but do not automatically isolate every shared dependency.
A schema-based encoding and interface toolchain. Field numbers carry wire identity, so contract evolution must preserve their meaning and avoid recycling removed numbers.
An ordered byte stream within a QUIC connection. Loss affecting one stream’s data need not block delivery of unrelated stream data, though congestion and shared resource limits still matter.
Behavior that depends on a harmful ordering of concurrent actions. A check followed later by a write can be unsafe even when both actions appear correct alone.
A stable position identifying the history already applied by a client. Recovery requires retained history or a defined snapshot fallback and fresh authorization.
An intermediary acting in front of servers. It can select an upstream, terminate TLS, or enforce request policy depending on its configured layer and capabilities.

Remote procedure call: an interface shaped as an operation on another process. Generated bindings reduce encoding work; they do not remove network delays, uncertain outcomes, or authorization requirements.
A method whose defined semantics are essentially read-only. Safety and idempotence are distinct properties; neither is a claim that a broken implementation cannot mutate state.
A learner’s own evaluation of submitted reasoning against a rubric. This academy labels it separately from objective quiz results and model-generated feedback.
A server-to-client event stream over HTTP. Reconnect metadata can help resume delivery, but the application must supply retention and replay semantics.
An explicit model used to explore consequences under stated assumptions. Its generated output is illustrative and must not be presented as measured production performance.

Service-level indicator: a measured description of user-visible service behavior, with a defined population and measurement window. Successful eligible requests divided by all eligible requests is one possible availability SLI.
Service-level objective: a target for a specified SLI over a window. The SLI says what is measured; the SLO says what result is acceptable.
The explicitly designated authority for a fact or state transition. A cache, search index, or projection is commonly derived and must have a recovery or reconciliation plan.
A value that does not include some newer authoritative update. Whether serving it is acceptable depends on the operation’s freshness and correctness contract.
A transport providing a reliable ordered byte stream within a connection. Applications still define message boundaries, deadlines, and what successful business completion means.
An execution path within a process. Threads commonly share process memory, so concurrent access to mutable state needs an explicit synchronization strategy.
The amount of completed work per unit time. Distinguish offered arrivals, accepted work, successful completions, and rejected requests.
The endpoint that decrypts a TLS connection. Plaintext is available there, so its identity, access, logging, and any next network hop belong in the trust model.
Time to live. Its meaning depends on the mechanism. In a cache, it limits how long a stored response may be reused under the applicable policy; it does not push an update to every reader.
Increasing resources available to an instance. It can simplify operations but retains instance limits and its failure domain.
A bidirectional message channel over a persistent connection. It provides neither durable message history nor offline delivery by itself.
A set of explicit assumptions about users, arrival rates, request mix, object sizes, skew, and growth. Estimates should expose the assumptions that could change the architecture.
